title: Custom vs premade engine?
author: toiletman74
selftext:
I was wondering which is better for coding agents (I personally use a local agent) making a custom engine or using premade engines (like godot, unity, etc..)

The reason I was wondering is becaise after having my local agent work with godot I've noticed that it spends a lot of time trying to use built in functions but using them wrong and having to troubleshoot. It wastes a ton of time. I can't exactly put all of godot's documentation into my agent's context so it doesn't seem like it would be easy to give it a better understanding of godot. But maybe a custom engine would be easier for it to understand since the code could fit in it's context easier? I've also seen quite a few people posting about making custom engines lately. 

Anyway if you have any recommendations or input on the subject I would appreciate it

replies.author: wadrasil
replies.body:
Its not impossible to have a somewhat automated pipeline.  

I was using omp and a fork of Claude/Codex game studio and a godot mcp with an LLM router and it was able to write the code; test in godot and try again. 

Omp was driving bitrouter via its bro code codex functionality by using the port of Claude/codex game studio.

I had it working on porting a python app to a godot app. 
It's not fast but it took a less time to port the app that it took me to write it. 

As far as what you can do today it is pretty trivial to take text from an old tabletop RPG and have ai make it into a app or game. 

Though it's not going to be a triple AAA game. But something you can use to entertain yourself.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
You’ll be missing really basic stuff if you try to build a purpose-built engine in a week.

Sure, you could make a game with 3d models and textures and things. But you’ll be missing a decent level editor and a ton of other really basic stuff. You can make something that looks good enough for a screenshot, but not something you actually want to use (if you know what you’re missing).

That’s why you see a lot of the same problems and same game types with vibe coded games. People are trying to do stuff like just use procedural generation for everything, to cover for the fact that it’s too difficult to make an ordinary level by hand.

replies.author: zenmatrix83
replies.body: My point is you can get a playable engine in a week and keep adding to it as you need to, and only feature you need as need them. In a week I had an engine up with an editor and input where I can walk around and interact with things which is the basis for most games. That’s with a. 20x plan running mostly non stop

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
Sure, you can get a playable engine in a week, but for most games, you want something a lot more than a ‘playable engine’ just to start figuring out basic game design issues.

A lot of these projects I see here kind of dodge the question. Maybe people make yet another Minecraft or No Man’s Sky clone, or a roguelike. A lot of games which are heavy on systems, like city builders.

If you have (1) prior game development experience and (2) an off the shelf engine like Unity, you’re getting a massive head start. If you just want to do everything with agents it will narrow your choices somewhat.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
TBH sounds like you’re using agents wrong, if that’s what you’re getting in Unity or Godot. The game engines have APIs, if you want the agent to do something best done with custom code, use the API for it and write the code.

Or think about it this way: before agents, let’s say that your game is 50% coding and 50% human touch. Now that agents have made the coding way faster,  you want an engine, because that speeds up the slowest part, which is the human touch.

replies.author: zenmatrix83
replies.body: no I've made games with them just fine, I've just seen massive improvements with how quickly an agent can solve a problem when it can just look at the code. even recent models still make too many assumptions and doing go and physically check apis references. and its just constant loops of fining issues to only notice it finnaly recognized it used the wrong name for a specific feature. using a existing engine will work fine and does, but I think if you can handle dealing with the engine side you can get much better results, but that takes more effort, but the timeline to a shippable product isn't as big as you think. You don't need to code everything, there are opensource model loaders and other things, and jolt physics engine is the same one you can use in other engines like godot.

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
I guess if your agents don’t work well for you in Unity, I can understand why you wouldn’t use them. I’m sure we have very different workflows. 

I still think engines give you a massive advantage most of the time—that’s based on my own experiences building with an without engines, and based on observations of the kind of problems I see in vibe coded games posted here.

replies.author: Anipixels
replies.body:
Fair to be sceptical, but no Godot and nothing from Minecraft. The only outside libraries are Silk.NET (it just opens the window and talks to OpenGL and the sound card) and a couple of audio decoders. Everything else is Claude's own C#: the renderer, chunk meshing, lighting, shadows, physics and collision, the audio mixer, UI, world generation and save files.
"An hour" was me exaggerating. The first working version, engine plus the game up to early hardmode, came together over the first evening, about 18k lines. It's had 18 days of work since, and the graphics code alone is about 150k lines now.
The Godot comparison is apples to oranges, though. Godot is a general-purpose engine: an editor, a scripting language, exports to every platform, physics for any genre. This is a game-specific engine that only does what one voxel game on Windows needs. Studios built engines like that for decades before Unity existed. It's a much smaller target, and that's what makes it doable.  Also the terrain in my game deforms more like valehim, and dirt and stone grows outward instead of being blocks but things you build with are blocks just like terraria.

replies.author: MrNotmark
replies.body:
Let me rephrase what I said, when I mentioned pulling Minecraft code, i did not mean that it would pull Minecraft code into your own game, that's written in java it is a different beast.
What I meant that Minecraft solved most of the things you're describing and the way I see your game, it is using the same concept.
Minecraft was built by one guy. Because the engine itself is very very simple. You just put down a bunch of blocks create chunks do some simple raycasting and voila you have a game.
Your game I would say uses the same concepts. It makes the terrain smooth but that is just a smooth modifier placed on top or a shader, the game is still using blocks right? 
Creating a blocky game engine like Minecraft is fairy simple and the AI has access to those codes because it was done a million times before by hobby gamedevs. So when I said it pulled Minecraft core I meant that the engine itself is a solved engine.

Now is that something that you could do in godot? Absolutely, it is fairly straightforward there as well I also built a voxel based game before there and didn't need 150k lines for graphics rendering.

The fact that claude built the lighting, shadow and physics is pretty impressive for the AI and it sounds like an interesting project. Hopefully you learnt a lot from that, otherwise if you did not learn from it and just built an engine, then... Why not make it in godot? You would've got the same things basically, Godot doesn't stop you from making voxel blocks.

replies.author: Anipixels
replies.body:
That's fair, and you're right on most of it. It's blocks underneath, a block engine is a well-solved problem, and Claude has seen plenty of them. That's a big part of why the first version came together so fast. I also need to correct my own number: about 127k of those 150k lines are the creature and item models and their textures, all made in code. The renderer itself is closer to 25k.
Why not Godot: honestly, it would have worked. The reason it ended up custom is testing. The game can start hundreds of hidden copies of itself from the command line, for about 900 automated tests, a bot that plays through the game, and frame-by-frame speed comparisons against real Terraria. Owning the whole loop made that easy for the AI, and everything is plain code it can read and check. And I'll be honest, I'm not a game dev. I direct it and playtest, so the learning has mostly been about how to run a project like this.

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body:
For many projects AI will work better with a custom engine because it owns the entire stack. You can see this in the extreme workflow efficiency when using threejs for example. Problem is, now say you want to go from a prototype game to an actual commercial release. Do you really want to own the entire engine? How will you actually test your renderer to make sure all the math is right? How will you add robust networking? How will you make sure a 5 year old AMD GPU doesn’t hit an obscure bug when you don’t even have the hardware to test on? How will you port to console should you get that far?

My plan was to transition from threejs to a custom C++ engine to preserve high velocity AI workflows but as my game started getting more complex, I had to ask myself all the questions above and I realized owning your own engine is a terrible proposition for a commercial game made by a solo dev. AI can write the engine in days, that doesn’t make maintenance free and that doesn’t prevent the long tail of obscure bugs (especially platform specific ones) from bitting you in the ass.

My compromise is going to be to keep my art pipeline almost entirely out of the engine, build full levels in blender with collision geometry and only final look, lighting, and shaders need in engine testing. I also may keep my full simulation engine separate from engine so I can run headless tests without loading the full engine. I’m still working all this out and deciding between porting to Unreal or Unity, so I’m just planning to stay in threejs for another month or two while I learn more.

I would say anything that has real hardware testing requirements, like rendering is very risky to own yourself unless you plan to setup a diverse test lab at home. AI works best when it can easily do full verification in a tight loop. Also anything with very complex math but subtle visual or gameplay differences is a big verification risk. You can own physics, but how will you know the math isn’t just a tad off? You can own rendering but how will you know the lighting calculations aren’t just slightly wrong?

comments.author: Zenity07
comments.body:
My recommendation for Godot is to instruct the agent to use it as a runtime only, basically ignore the editor, and prefer building non-trivial features as C++ engine modules or GD extensions. Don't use binary installations of Godot but give it the full source code. You are basically getting most of the benefits of a custom engine but without starting from zero.

I still prefer starting with Godot for most projects, unless your needs are very specific then the custom engine approach is perfectly reasonable as well and sometimes better. Though you should really know what you are doing then and what to ask for.
